  "text": "The laundromat had one machine nobody used.

Number nine.

Its window was painted white from the inside, and someone had scratched DON'T COUNT into the coin slot.

At midnight, with every other washer occupied, I put my clothes in it.

The paint was gone now.

I counted seven shirts, three pairs of trousers, eleven socks.

Twenty-one things.

The machine started before I inserted any money.

Halfway through the cycle, something knocked against the glass.

A hand.

I stepped back.

It was my hand. The little scar across the thumb, the crooked finger I'd broken at twelve.

It pressed against the window, then disappeared into the foam.

The attendant emerged from behind a curtain.

“How many?” she asked.

I couldn't answer.

“How many did you put in?”

“Twenty-one.”

She closed her eyes.

Inside the washer, somebody began counting.

My voice, muffled by water.

“One. Two. Three.”

The attendant unplugged the machine.

It kept turning.

“Listen carefully,” she said. “When it stops, take your clothes. Nothing else. Whatever you recognize.”

The counting reached twenty-one.

The door clicked open.

My clothes lay folded inside, perfectly dry.

Beneath them was a photograph of my father holding a baby.

On the back, in his handwriting: Our second try.

I had always been an only child.

Behind the drum, someone whispered, “Twenty-two.”

The attendant caught my wrist before I reached in.

Outside, I checked the bag.

Seven shirts. Three trousers. Eleven socks.

My phone rang.

Dad.

For a long time he listened to me breathing.

Then he asked, “Which one came out?”"
